title: The Case for Logging Every Workout
excerpt: Memory rounds up and forgets the bad weeks. How a simple training log tells the truth, what to record, and how to use it to plan your next session.
description: Memory rounds up and forgets bad weeks. A simple training log tells the truth. What to record, how to keep it under a minute, and how it guides your next session.

toc.title: Your Memory Is a Terrible Training Partner
Let the Log Make Your Decisions

bodyHtml:
Your Memory Is a Terrible Training Partner

Ask yourself what you deadlifted for five reps six weeks ago. Or how long Cindy took you last spring. Most of us get close, and "close" is where the trouble starts. We remember the good days sharper than the average ones, round numbers up, and quietly forget the weeks we skipped.

A training log fixes that without asking much of you. It turns "I think I'm getting stronger" into "I added 15 pounds to my squat in two months." That difference matters most when you train alone in a garage, because nobody else is watching your progress. The log is the only witness you have.

"When you train alone, the log is the only witness to your progress."

What to Write Down

You do not need a spreadsheet with forty columns. For each session, a handful of facts covers nearly everything you will want later:

  • The date and what the workout was (name, format, time cap)
  • Loads, rep schemes, and any scaling you used
  • Your result: time, rounds, or total reps
  • One line on how it felt, such as "grip gave out in round 3" or "easy, could have pushed"

That last line is the one people skip, and it is often the most useful. Numbers tell you what happened. The note tells you why. Six months from now, "slept badly, 4 hours" explains a slow time better than any amount of squinting at the result.

Keep It Under a Minute

The log you keep is the one that is easy to fill in. If recording a workout takes ten minutes, you will stop by the second week. Aim for under a minute, right after you finish, while you are still sweaty and the numbers are fresh.

Use whatever fits your habits. A whiteboard on the garage wall works. So does a cheap notebook that lives next to the rack. The best method is the one that is already in reach when you finish your last rep.

Try this: Log before you cool down. Once the numbers are written, the session is officially over. Tying the log to a habit you already have makes it stick far better than good intentions do.

Let the Log Make Your Decisions

Here is where logging starts paying you back. Once you have a few weeks of entries, you stop guessing about your training and start reading it.

Not sure whether to go RX or scale? Look at what you did last time and how it felt. Our post on choosing RX or scaled weights walks through that decision, and a log makes it nearly automatic. Want to know if you are actually improving at a benchmark? Retest it and compare, which is the whole idea behind test and retest. Wondering why you feel flat this week? Scroll back and check whether you have done five hard days in a row.

It also takes the pressure off programming. If you build sessions with the WOD Builder or grab the Daily 20 on a busy day, your log shows you which movements you keep hitting and which ones you keep dodging. Most people are surprised by that second list.

Log the Bad Days Too

The temptation is to record only the wins. A new PR gets written down in ink, and the day you fell apart in round two gets quietly skipped. That makes the log flattering and nearly useless.

The rough sessions carry the best information. They show you patterns: always fading on days you train fasted, always struggling after a poor night of sleep, always dreading the same movement. They also make your good stretches mean more. A log with honest lows lets you see how far the average has climbed, which is the thing that keeps you training through a flat month.

Short sessions count, too. A ten-minute minimum-day workout on a crazy week still goes in the book. A history without gaps tells the truth about who you are as an athlete: someone who kept showing up.

Start With Your Next Workout

You do not need to go back and reconstruct the last year. Pick your next session, write down the basics, and add one line about how it felt. Do that for four weeks and look at what you have. You will likely find something you did not expect, whether that is a lift that quietly climbed, a movement you avoid, or a pattern in your best days.

If you want somewhere to start, browse the workout library and pick a benchmark you can repeat later. A logged baseline today is the easiest win you will give your future self.
